findings.title: Input-port node created before child-membership filter -> orphan port nodes (asymmetric with output-port handling)
findings.description: In handleDrillIntoSubmodel, the input-port construction creates a SUBMODEL_PORT node for every parent source (line 120) and only afterwards filters which child edges to draw with `if (!childIds.has(childId)) continue` (line 127). The output-port construction does the opposite: it applies the membership filter during grouping (line 146 `if (!childIds.has(childId)) continue`) and additionally requires `e.sourceHandle` (line 141), so a target with no valid in-submodel children never enters `outputsByTarget` and no orphan output port is created. Because of this asymmetry, any parent edge that targets the submodel node but resolves to a childId not present in the submodel (e.g. `targetHandle` missing -> childId becomes the sentinel `"__unconnected__"`, line 111; or a stale `in__<id>` handle after edit/dissolve/re-create cycles) still produces an input port node (`port_in__<srcId>`) with zero connecting edges. That orphan node is passed to getLayoutedElements and rendered with no edges. There is no later pruning of edge-less port nodes.
findings.evidence: Input branch: inputsBySource groups e.source -> childIds (including "__unconnected__" sentinel). For each srcId it unconditionally `newNodes.push(validateReactFlowNode({id: port_in__<srcId>, ...}))` (120-125), THEN loops children with `if (!childIds.has(childId)) continue` (126-127). So a source whose only target child is "__unconnected__" (or any non-member id) yields a port node but no edge. Output branch filters first (146 `if (!childIds.has(childId)) continue` before adding to outputsByTarget), so no equivalent orphan output port is ever created. Symmetric fix would skip creating the input port when none of its targetChildIds are in childIds.

findings.title: GPU VRAM estimate scaled by wrong denominator (safe_row_limit instead of total_rows), overstating VRAM whenever RAM downsampling applies
findings.description: The reactive `adjusted` memo rescales the backend's `gpu_vram_estimated_mb` to the user's effective GPU row count, but uses `originalRows = safe_row_limit ?? sourceRows` as the baseline the backend estimate was computed at. The backend actually computes that estimate at `total_rows` (full source rows), NOT at `safe_row_limit`. So whenever `was_downsampled` is true (i.e. `safe_row_limit < total_rows`), the displayed GPU VRAM is inflated by a factor of `sourceRows / safe_row_limit`. This also feeds the warning banner at lines 170-177 ("GPU training needs ~X but GPU has Y. Training will fall back to CPU automatically."), so a spurious CPU-fallback warning can be shown to the user even when the GPU could actually fit the workload.
findings.evidence: Backend: src/haute/routes/modelling.py:196 sets `effective_rows = ram_est.total_rows or 0` and line 203 calls `_check_gpu_vram(effective_rows, ...)`, whose result populates `gpu_vram_estimated_mb` (line 218). So the baseline row count for the estimate is `total_rows == sourceRows`. Frontend TrainingActionsAndResults.tsx: line 76 `gpuRows = hasUserLimit ? Math.min(rowLimit, sourceRows) : sourceRows`; line 77 `originalRows = ramEstimate.safe_row_limit ?? sourceRows`; line 79 `gpuVramMb = gpuVramMb * gpuRows / originalRows`. Case: total_rows=100000, safe_row_limit=50000 (was_downsampled), no user rowLimit -> gpuRows=100000, originalRows=50000, gpuRows!==originalRows so it scales B*100000/50000 = 2*B, doubling the estimate the backend already computed for 100000 rows. With a user limit L: scales B*min(L,source)/safe_row_limit instead of the correct B*min(L,source)/sourceRows, still overstated by sourceRows/safe_row_limit. The correct denominator is `total_rows` (sourceRows). Not covered by TrainingActionsAndResults.test.tsx (no test sets gpu_vram_estimated_mb together with safe_row_limit).

findings.title: buildExecutionFailureMessage drops UI options when delegating to buildExecutionDiagnostic, silently suppressing the memory diagnostic when metrics.status is a non-memory terminal reason
findings.description: buildExecutionFailureMessage decides a failure is memory-limited via isMemoryLimitedFailure(metrics, resolvedOptions), which considers options.status / options.terminalReason / options.errorCode in addition to metrics.terminal_reason. But when it then builds the human message it calls buildExecutionDiagnostic(metrics) WITHOUT forwarding resolvedOptions. Inside, shouldShowMemoryPressureDiagnostic(metrics, {}) re-derives the memory signal using only metrics.* and, crucially, suppresses the diagnostic whenever metrics.status (or metrics.terminal_reason) is a non-memory terminal reason. So if the memory signal arrived via the explicit options.status='memory_limited' (e.g. job-level terminal reason) while the embedded metrics.status is 'error'/'contract_error'/'timed_out'/'cancelled'/'superseded', the outer guard passes (memory) but the inner re-check fails (non-memory), buildExecutionDiagnostic returns null, and the function falls back to the bare base message — dropping the memory-pressure detail the caller intended to surface.
findings.evidence: Line 199 guard: isMemoryLimitedFailure(metrics, resolvedOptions) — true when resolvedOptions.status='memory_limited'. Line 203: buildExecutionDiagnostic(metrics) — options NOT passed. buildExecutionDiagnostic -> shouldShowMemoryPressureDiagnostic(metrics, {}) (line 174). With options={}, isMemoryLimitedFailure(metrics,{}) checks only metrics.terminal_reason; then lines 162-163 isNonMemoryTerminalReason(metrics.terminal_reason)/isNonMemoryTerminalReason(metrics.status) return true if metrics.status is e.g. 'error' -> returns false -> diagnostic null -> line 204 returns baseMessage?.trim()||prefix. The existing test at executionDiagnostics.test.ts:111 only survives because the fixture default metrics.status='running' (non-terminal); the divergent metrics.status='error' case is untested and regresses to the generic message.

findings.title: setSources can leave activeSource pointing at a non-existent 'live' source, breaking the invariant removeSource enforces
findings.description: setSources resets activeSource to the literal 'live' whenever the incoming list does not contain the current activeSource (line 166). This assumes 'live' is always a member of the new list, but setSources accepts an arbitrary array and does not guarantee/insert 'live'. Calling setSources with a list that omits 'live' (e.g. setSources(['foo'])) leaves activeSource='live' referencing a source that is not in sources. removeSource deliberately hard-blocks removing 'live' (line 177) to preserve exactly this invariant, so the two setters are asymmetric: the 'live-always-present' assumption baked into the fallback is enforced by removeSource but silently violable via setSources.
findings.evidence: Line 166: activeSource: sources.includes(s.activeSource) ? s.activeSource : 'live'. If sources=['foo'] and current activeSource='bar', result is activeSource='live' while sources has no 'live'. Contrast removeSource line 177: if (name==='live') return s (cannot remove live). The fallback target 'live' is never validated against the new sources array.

findings.title: Ctrl+Shift+Z / Cmd+Shift+Z redo is unreachable (contradictory key+shift check) — breaks keyboard redo, the only redo shortcut on macOS
findings.description: The redo branch requires `mod && e.key === "z" && e.shiftKey && !isTyping`. In every real browser, holding Shift changes the printable key value, so pressing Shift+Z yields `e.key === "Z"` (uppercase), never `"z"`. Therefore the condition `e.key === "z" && e.shiftKey` can never be simultaneously true: when `shiftKey` is true the key is `"Z"`. The standard redo accelerator Ctrl+Shift+Z (Windows/Linux) and Cmd+Shift+Z (macOS) is dead. On macOS there is no Ctrl+Y fallback (line 60 only helps Windows users), so keyboard redo is completely non-functional for Mac users. The undo branch at line 49 (`e.key === "z" && !e.shiftKey`) works because Ctrl alone does not alter the character.
findings.evidence: Line 49 undo: `if (mod && e.key === "z" && !e.shiftKey && !isTyping)`. Line 54 redo: `if (mod && e.key === "z" && e.shiftKey && !isTyping)`. Browser semantics: Shift+Z => KeyboardEvent.key === "Z". So line 54 is unreachable in real browsers; Cmd+Shift+Z on Mac matches NO handler (lines 49/54/60 all fail) => nothing happens, no preventDefault. The unit test (useKeyboardShortcuts.test.ts:67-70) fires `new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 'z', shiftKey: true })` — an artificial combination browsers never emit — so it passes while masking the real-browser breakage.
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a

findings.title: All letter-key shortcuts silently break when CapsLock is on (no e.key case normalization)
findings.description: Every letter shortcut compares the raw `e.key` against a lowercase literal: Ctrl+S (`"s"`), Ctrl+Z (`"z"`), Ctrl+Y (`"y"`), Ctrl+C (`"c"`), Ctrl+V (`"v"`), Ctrl+A (`"a"`), Ctrl+K (`"k"`), Ctrl+G (`"g"`). When CapsLock is active, the browser reports the uppercase key value (e.g. `e.key === "S"`), so none of these comparisons match and every letter shortcut — including save, undo, copy, paste, select-all — silently stops working with no feedback. The handler never normalizes case (no `e.key.toLowerCase()`), so the behaviour depends on the user's CapsLock state. Shares a root cause with the Ctrl+Shift+Z bug: normalizing the key once (`const key = e.key.toLowerCase()`) fixes both.
findings.evidence: Line 42 `e.key === "s"`, line 49/54 `"z"`, line 60 `"y"`, line 67 `"c"`, line 81 `"v"`, line 122 `"a"`, line 136 `"k"`, line 157 `"g"`. No `toLowerCase()` anywhere in the file. CapsLock on => `e.key` is uppercase for letters => all these strict-equality checks fail. No test exercises uppercase keys (grep for `toLowerCase|getModifierState|key: "[A-Z]"` returns nothing in hook and test).
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a

findings.title: Paste generates colliding edge ids for parallel edges (id derived only from node ids, ignoring handles)
findings.description: When pasting copied nodes, each new edge id is built solely from the remapped source/target node ids: `id: `e-${newSource}-${newTarget}``. The copied edges spread `...ed` (retaining distinct `sourceHandle`/`targetHandle`), so a selection containing two parallel edges between the same node pair (e.g. an edgeJoin with `role-left`/`role-right` target handles, both fed from copies of the same upstream node) produces two new edges with identical ids. React Flow requires unique edge ids; duplicate ids cause one edge to be dropped or render incorrectly. The id should incorporate the handles (as the rest of the edge layer keys on sourceHandle/targetHandle — see useEdgeHandlers.ts:142-143, edgeJoinCanonicalTargetHandle).
findings.evidence: Line 113: `return [{ ...ed, id: `e-${newSource}-${newTarget}`, source: newSource, target: newTarget }]`. Two copied edges with same source/target node but different targetHandle (legal per useEdgeHandlers role handles) => same `newSource`/`newTarget` => identical generated id. Contrast: edge creation elsewhere preserves sourceHandle/targetHandle (useEdgeHandlers.ts:181-201) precisely because the pair is not unique.
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a

findings.title: useUIStore() subscribed without a selector forces App to re-render on every UI-store mutation
findings.description: The hook calls `const { setShortcutsOpen, setSubmodelDialog, setNodeSearchOpen } = useUIStore()` with no selector, subscribing the consuming component (App, the top-level component) to the entire UI store. Any UI-store change (hoveredNodeId, paletteOpen, nodePanelWidth, explorePanes, etc.) re-renders App even though this hook only ever needs three referentially-stable setters. The file is inconsistent with itself one line up — line 32 uses a selector (`useToastStore((s) => s.addToast)`). Because the setters are stable Zustand actions, a selector (or `useUIStore.getState()` inline, mirroring how the hook already reads `useUIStore.getState().nodeSearchOpen` at line 136) avoids the spurious subscription with no behavior change.

Store (useUIStore.ts:62) defines actions once in `create((set) => ({...}))` so they are stable; the no-selector subscription only adds re-renders. Line 32 already demonstrates the selector idiom; line 136 already uses `useUIStore.getState()` for one-off reads.
findings.est_reduction: ~1 line changed; removes whole-store subscription on the top-level App component
findings.behavior_preservation: Setters are stable store actions; reading them via a selector or getState yields identical references and identical handler behavior, only reducing re-render frequency.

findings.title: Error path sets columns to [] without updating prevColumnFingerprint, can wedge state empty against a later equal-schema cache
findings.description: The fetch .catch handler does `if (!cachedColumnsRef.current) setDataInputColumns([])` but never updates `prevColumnFingerprint.current`. Every OTHER place that calls setDataInputColumns first writes the new fingerprint into prevColumnFingerprint (lines 102, 111, 118, 127, 132, 156). After a no-cache error with a NON-empty `fallbackColumns`, state becomes [] while prevColumnFingerprint still holds fp(fallback). If the store cache is later populated externally with columns whose fingerprint equals that stale prev (e.g. the same schema as the fallback), the sync effect (lines 100-105) compares fp(cache) === prev and SKIPS the update, leaving the hook permanently returning [] even though valid cached columns now exist. The invariant 'prevColumnFingerprint mirrors the currently displayed columns' is silently broken only on this branch.
findings.evidence: Line 166 `if (!cachedColumnsRef.current) setDataInputColumns([])` with no accompanying `prevColumnFingerprint.current = columnFingerprint([])` (which would be the EMPTY_COLUMNS_FINGERPRINT "0:"). Contrast every successful update which pairs the setState with a prev write (e.g. lines 155-157). Reachability: requires `enabled` true with a non-empty `fallbackColumns` (so initial prev = fp(fallback), not "0:"), then a rejected fetch with no cache, then an external cache populate matching the fallback schema. The current sole caller (OptimiserConfig.tsx:277-280) only enables the hook when `fallbackDataInputColumns` is empty, so it avoids the trigger today, but the hook is a reusable public API and the missing fingerprint write is a genuine state-sync defect.

findings.title: readV2 silently downgrades an unknown column `type` to "str", defeating the backend's B1 loud-fail guardrail on editor round-trip
findings.description: readV2 coerces any column `type` that is not one of int|float|str|bool|date to "str" (the `ALLOWED_TYPES.has(...) ? cc.type : "str"` branch). The backend mirror `_api_input_schema.py` deliberately does the OPPOSITE: guardrail B1 (validate_v2_schema, lines 368-376) raises ApiInputSchemaError on an unknown type precisely because — per its own comment — 'Today's silent downgrade to str (in _json_shred.py) loses information; loud-fail ... forces the user to correct typos.' Because the editor reads via readV2 (ApiInputEditor.tsx:171,287-291) and persists via writeV2 (volatileSchema at :408 + save), a config that arrived with e.g. `type:"decimal"` is silently rewritten to `type:"str"`, which then PASSES B1. So any config opened+saved in the editor bypasses the very guardrail the backend added, with no user-visible signal (the type <select> at ApiInputEditor.tsx:717-729 just shows the already-coerced "str"). This contradicts CLAUDE.md's 'fail loudly' directive and the module's own claim that the strict serialiser only DROPS unknown keys (it also mutates a declared type here).
findings.evidence: apiInputSchema.ts:113-117 `typeof cc.type === "string" && ALLOWED_TYPES.has(cc.type as ColumnType) ? cc.type : "str"` vs _api_input_schema.py:369-376 `if not isinstance(ctype, str) or ctype not in _ALLOWED_COLUMN_TYPES: raise ApiInputSchemaError(...)`. The backend comment at lines 281-285 names the silent str-downgrade as the defect B1 exists to prevent; readV2 reintroduces it at the editor read layer. writeV2 (:170-177) emits the coerced `type` verbatim, so the mutation reaches disk.

findings.title: Histogram block dereferences edges[0]/edges[last] without a guard, unlike counts
findings.description: The scenario-value histogram IIFE guards counts (`if (!counts || counts.length === 0) return null`) but never guards `edges`. It then reads `eMin = edges[0]` and `eMax = edges[edges.length - 1]` and renders `eMin.toFixed(2)` (line 136) and `eMax.toFixed(2)` (line 140) unconditionally. If a payload ever has non-empty `counts` but empty/short `edges`, both `eMin` and `eMax` are `undefined` and `undefined.toFixed(2)` throws a TypeError, crashing the whole SummaryTab render (an uncaught error in render, not a localized fallback).
findings.evidence: Line 114 guards only counts: `if (!counts || counts.length === 0) return null`. Lines 119-120: `const eMin = edges[0], eMax = edges[edges.length - 1]`. The Pydantic wire schema `OptimiserScenarioValueHistogram` (src/haute/schemas.py:1135-1137) declares `counts: list[int] = Field(default_factory=list)` and `edges: list[float] = Field(default_factory=list)` — both default to empty independently, and the frontend type marks `edges: number[]` as required without enforcing the implicit N+1 length relationship to `counts`. The producing code (`_compute_scenario_value_stats`, _optimiser_service.py:1315) emits counts(20)/edges(21) together, so the mismatch is not reachable via current backend output; this is a latent robustness gap / contract-trust asymmetry rather than a live crash. The `oneX` computation (line 120) already degrades safely to null for empty edges, but the axis labels do not.

findings.title: Constraint-met derivation duplicated verbatim with DetailCard

The repo already factors constraint logic into optimiserHelpers (`isConstraintMet`); the surrounding spec-key extraction belongs there too. findings.title: Best-iteration reference line treats best_iteration as an array index, misplacing it when loss_history is truncated
findings.description: `bestX` is computed as `xScale(Math.min(Math.max(bestIteration, 0), lossHistory.length - 1))`, but `xScale(i) = marginLeft + (i / (length-1)) * chartW` interprets its argument as a 0-based ARRAY INDEX into `lossHistory`, whereas `result.best_iteration` is the model's actual ITERATION NUMBER. These coincide only when `loss_history` starts at iteration 0 and is 1:1 with its index. The backend (`_train_service.py` `_bounded_loss_history`, default `HAUTE_TRAIN_LOSS_HISTORY_LIMIT=200`) keeps only the last 200 rows (`history[-200:]`) for runs longer than 200 iterations, so the window slides and `lossHistory[0].iteration` is non-zero (e.g. iterations 700..899 for a 900-iteration run). In that case a `best_iteration` of, say, 750 is clamped to `min(750, 199)=199` and the dashed best line is drawn at the far RIGHT edge while the x-axis labels (which correctly render `lossHistory[idx].iteration`) and the legend (`Best iteration (750)`) point elsewhere — a misleading model-diagnostic. findings.title: Stale-response race: out-of-order getRuns/getModelVersions can overwrite current data
findings.description: refreshRuns and refreshVersions fire an un-cancellable fetch and unconditionally apply the result in .then. The fetch guard (fetchedRunsFor / fetchedVersionsFor) only prevents duplicate in-flight fetches for the SAME key; it does not discard a response for a stale key. When the user switches experiments, MlflowModelPicker (ExperimentRunPicker onChange, MlflowModelPicker.tsx:182-184) calls setRuns([]), resetRunsGuard(), then refreshRuns(newExpId). If the previous getRuns(oldExpId) is still in flight, its .then runs setRuns(oldData) whenever it resolves and can land AFTER the new experiment's data, leaving the dropdown showing runs from the wrong experiment. Same pattern for refreshVersions on a fast model switch. getRuns/getModelVersions already accept an AbortSignal (api/client.ts:1032,1047) but the hook never passes one nor tracks a request id, so there is no last-write-wins protection.
findings.evidence: refreshRuns: fetchedRunsFor.current = expId; getRuns(expId, runTag).then(data => setRuns(...)). No signal, no per-call sequence check. resetRunsGuard() clears the guard so a slow prior request's .then is no longer even gated. Consumer switches exp -> two getRuns promises in flight -> whichever resolves last wins, not whichever was requested last.

findings.title: Mount effect that resets fetch-guard refs is a no-op
findings.description: The useEffect with [] dependency reassigns fetchedExperiments/fetchedModels/fetchedRunsFor/fetchedVersionsFor to false/"" on mount. But these refs are created with useRef(false)/useRef(""), which already initializes them to exactly those values, and React creates fresh ref objects for every new component instance (i.e. after any unmount+remount). At the first render of every mount the refs already hold their initial values, so the effect writes the values they already have. The comment 'Reset all fetch guards on mount so data is re-fetched after remount' describes behavior that remount provides for free; the effect adds nothing.
findings.evidence: const fetchedExperiments = useRef(false) ... useEffect(() => { fetchedExperiments.current = false; fetchedModels.current = false; fetchedRunsFor.current = ""; fetchedVersionsFor.current = "" }, []). On remount React calls useRef(false) again -> new ref initialized to false; the effect sets it to false again.
findings.est_reduction: ~7 lines
findings.behavior_preservation: Removing the effect leaves identical runtime behavior: refs are already false/empty at first render of every mount.

findings.title: Unreachable NaN guard in updateCell push branch
findings.description: updateCell computes num = val === "" ? safeDefault : (Number.isNaN(parsed) ? safeDefault : parsed). safeDefault comes from resolveDefault(), which is guaranteed non-NaN (returns 1 on NaN). parsed is only used when it is not NaN. So num is always a finite number. The new-entry push then writes value: Number.isNaN(num) ? 0 : num, but Number.isNaN(num) can never be true, so the ': num' branch is the only reachable one and the '0' fallback is dead.
findings.evidence: Line 67: const num = val === "" ? safeDefault : (Number.isNaN(parsed) ? safeDefault : parsed). Line 70: next.push({ [factor]: level, value: Number.isNaN(num) ? 0 : num }). num cannot be NaN -> fallback 0 unreachable; the map branch (line 68) correctly uses num directly without the guard, confirming intent.
findings.est_reduction: 1 expression simplified to `value: num`

findings.title: CI whiskers can overflow the bar container because maxDev ignores confidence-interval bounds
findings.description: The horizontal scale `maxDev` is derived ONLY from each term's point deviation `|relativity - 1|` (with a 0.1 floor). The confidence-interval whiskers are then positioned/sized against this same `maxDev`. Because a relativity's CI is frequently WIDER than the largest point-deviation across the displayed terms, `ci_lower`/`ci_upper` routinely fall outside the `[1 - maxDev, 1 + maxDev]` range, producing a whisker with negative `left` (overflowing left, past the feature-name column) and/or `width` > 100% (extending past the right edge). The bar container (line 91, `className="flex-1 h-4 relative"`) has no `overflow: hidden`, so the overflow is visible and the whisker is clipped/misplaced, misrepresenting the displayed uncertainty.
findings.evidence: Line 45: `const maxDev = Math.max(rows.map(r => Math.abs(r.relativity - 1)).reduce((a,b)=>Math.max(a,b), -Infinity), 0.1)` — only point deviations feed maxDev. Lines 116-117 scale the whisker against maxDev: `left: ${50 + ((row.ci_lower - 1) / maxDev) * 50}%` and `width: ${((row.ci_upper - row.ci_lower) / maxDev) * 50}%`. Worked example: a single term with relativity=1.05 (dev 0.05 → maxDev floored to 0.1) and CI [0.7, 1.5] yields whisker left = 50 + ((0.7-1)/0.1)*50 = -100% and width = ((1.5-0.7)/0.1)*50 = 400%. The point bar itself never overflows (pct = (|dev|/maxDev)*50 ≤ 50 since maxDev ≥ |dev|), so the defect is whisker-specific. Container at line 91 has no overflow clipping.

findings.title: Unreachable defensive branch coerces non-numeric relativity to dev=0, inconsistent with the rest of the component
findings.description: `const dev = typeof row.relativity === 'number' ? row.relativity - 1 : 0` defends against `relativity` not being a number, but the wire contract guarantees it always is: the TrainResult type declares `glm_relativities: { feature: string; relativity: number; ... }[]` (relativity is a required `number`), and the backend runs `_assert_json_finite(response)` over the whole train response (routes/_train_service.py:1147 and routes/modelling.py:78), which RAISES on any non-finite numeric rather than emitting a sentinel. So `row.relativity` is always a finite number when rows are populated, making the `: 0` branch unreachable. The branch is also internally inconsistent: the very same `row.relativity` is used WITHOUT this guard in the sort comparator (lines 30-31, `b.relativity - a.relativity` / `Math.abs(b.relativity - 1)`), which correctly assumes it is always a number. Worse, were the impossible case to occur, this branch would silently place the bar exactly on the baseline (dev=0) instead of failing loudly, contrary to the project's no-silent-fallback guidance.
findings.evidence: Type at frontend/src/stores/useNodeResultsStore.ts:73 `glm_relativities?: { feature: string; relativity: number; ci_lower?: number; ci_upper?: number }[]`. Backend finiteness gate: src/haute/routes/_train_service.py:338-341 raises `ValueError("non-finite numeric value at {path}")`. The dead branch (line 75) contradicts the unguarded numeric use at lines 30-31 of the same prop.
findings.est_reduction: ~1 line simplified (drop the ternary, use `const dev = row.relativity - 1`)
findings.behavior_preservation: Behavior is identical for all inputs permitted by the wire contract (finite numeric relativity); only the unreachable non-number path changes, and removing it aligns with fail-loud policy.

findings.title: handleSort default-direction ternary has two identical branches (no-op conditional, intended numeric-desc default lost)
findings.description: When switching the active sort to a NEW column, the code computes the new sort direction with `setSortDir(key === "feature" ? "asc" : "asc")`. Both arms of the ternary evaluate to the literal `"asc"`, so the condition `key === "feature"` is computed and then discarded — it has zero effect on the result. The shape of the expression (a ternary keyed on whether the column is the text column `feature` vs the numeric columns coefficient/std_error/z_value/p_value) strongly indicates the author intended numeric statistic columns to default to descending order (largest-magnitude / most-significant first, the conventional default for a coefficients table), while the text `feature` column defaults to ascending. As written that intent is silently dropped: every freshly selected column always starts ascending, so e.g. clicking the `Estimate` or `z` header first shows the smallest values at the top rather than the largest. There is no incorrect state — just a dead conditional plus a missing feature.
findings.evidence: Line 63-70 handleSort: `if (sortKey === key) { setSortDir(d => d === "asc" ? "desc" : "asc") } else { setSortKey(key); setSortDir(key === "feature" ? "asc" : "asc") }`. The else-branch ternary returns "asc" for both true and false, so `key === "feature"` is evaluated and thrown away. Contrast with the numeric vs string handling that exists in the `sorted` comparator (localeCompare for strings, numeric subtraction otherwise), confirming the two column families are meant to behave differently.
findings.est_reduction: Collapse to `setSortDir("asc")` (or implement the intended `key === "feature" ? "asc" : "desc"`); removes a dead conditional (~1 line of pointless branching).
findings.behavior_preservation: Replacing the ternary with the constant `"asc"` is exactly behavior-preserving (both arms already return "asc"). If instead the intended numeric-desc default is restored, behavior changes only in the initial sort direction when a numeric column is first selected — no data/values change, only ordering of an already-sortable table.

findings.title: Duplicating a node copies the original's cached preview/result fields (_columns, _availableColumns, _schemaWarnings, _status, _traceValue) into the duplicate, violating the clearCachedResultShape invariant
findings.description: handleDuplicateNode builds the new node's data with a shallow spread `data: { ...original.data, label: ... }`. This carries over ALL runtime/cached fields the original accumulated from its last preview/run: `_columns`, `_availableColumns`, `_schemaWarnings`, `_status`, `_traceValue`, `_traceActive`, etc. (defined on HauteNodeData in types/node.ts). The duplicate has a brand-new id with NO cached result in useNodeResultsStore, yet its `data` advertises the original's columns and an `_status: "ok"`. Downstream this is user-visible: ColumnsTab is fed `availableColumns`/`columns` derived from these `_*` fields, so the freshly duplicated (never-run) node shows the original's schema and lets the user edit `selected_columns` against stale columns; the node also renders as already-succeeded. The codebase already encodes the opposite invariant: NodePanel.handleConfigUpdate wraps every config write in `clearCachedResultShape()` (NodePanel.tsx:567-573, deleting _columns/_availableColumns/_schemaWarnings) precisely because a node whose identity/config changed must not keep stale cached schema. handleCreateInstance (same file, lines 94-105) constructs `data` from scratch with no `_*` fields, so duplicate is the inconsistent outlier. Secondary: the shallow spread also makes `newNode.data.config` the SAME object reference as `original.data.config`; the normal edit path replaces config immutably so this is currently latent, but any in-place config mutation would corrupt both nodes.
findings.evidence: Lines 75-81: `const newNode: Node = { ...original, id: newId, position: {...}, selected: true, data: { ...original.data, label: `${original.data.label} copy` } }`. `original.data` includes _columns/_availableColumns/_schemaWarnings/_status (HauteNodeData). No call to clearCachedResultShape or stripping of `_*` keys. Compare NodePanel.tsx:616 `onUpdateNode(id, clearCachedResultShape({ ...currentNode.data, config: newConfig }))` and useNodeHandlers handleCreateInstance which sets `data: { label, description, nodeType, config }` only.

findings.title: Stale (ghost) entries in selected_columns inflate the toggle count, causing 'select one column' to silently revert to all-selected and pull in unrelated real columns
findings.description: When selected_columns contains names that are no longer in the current schema (the component's own first-class 'stale ghost rows' feature, rendered with the '(not found)' suffix), those stale names still live inside `selectedColumns`. In toggleColumn's add-branch, `const next = [...selectedColumns, col]` includes the stale entries, and the all-selected revert guard `if (next.length >= allColumns.length)` compares this inflated length against `allColumns.length` (which EXCLUDES stale columns). The stale entries can push `next.length` to `>= allColumns.length` before the user has actually selected every real column, so toggling a single real column ON silently flips the node back to empty (= keep all columns), thereby selecting other real columns the user never checked and dropping the explicit list. Example: allColumns=[a,b,c], selected_columns=["a","stale1"]; user checks `b` -> next=["a","stale1","b"], length 3 >= 3 -> onUpdate('selected_columns', []) -> a,b,AND c are now kept. Column `c` was never selected by the user. The length comparison should be against the count of REAL selected columns (filtered through allColumnNames), not the raw array that includes ghosts.
findings.evidence: Lines 57-64: `const next = [...selectedColumns, col]; if (next.length >= allColumns.length) { onUpdate('selected_columns', []) } else { onUpdate('selected_columns', next) }`. `selectedColumns` may contain stale names (staleColumns is built at lines 28-33 from exactly `selectedColumns.filter(name => !allColumnNames.has(name))`), so `next.length` over-counts relative to `allColumns.length` which is derived from availableColumns/columns with no stale entries.

findings.title: selectedCount counts stale ghost columns, so the 'N / total' badge can read e.g. '3 / 3' when only 1 real column is actually selected
findings.description: selectedCount uses `selectedColumns.length` in the explicit (non-all) case, but selectedColumns can include stale names not present in allColumns. The denominator of the badge is `allColumns.length`, which excludes stale entries. The result is a count that double-misleads: the numerator is inflated by ghost columns while the denominator excludes them, so the badge can display the count of selected as equal to or greater than the real total. Example: allColumns=[a,b,c], selected_columns=["a","stale1","stale2"] -> isAllSelected=false, selectedCount=3, badge shows '3 / 3', implying every output column is selected, when in fact only `a` is a real selected output column and b,c are deselected. The count should be the number of selectedColumns that are also in allColumnNames (real, kept columns).
findings.evidence: Line 77: `const selectedCount = isAllSelected ? allColumns.length : selectedColumns.length`. Badge lines 93-95: `{selectedCount} / {allColumns.length}`. staleColumns (lines 28-33) proves selectedColumns can contain names absent from allColumnNames; those are counted by selectedColumns.length but not by allColumns.length.

findings.title: ModellingPreview passes config={{}} to SummaryTab, silently dropping the user's MLflow experiment_name and model_name on export
findings.description: ModellingPreview renders <SummaryTab ... config={{}} />. SummaryTab forwards `config` into MlflowExportSection, which derives the MLflow request fields via configField(config, "mlflow_experiment", "") and configField(config, "model_name", ""). Because an empty object is passed, both lookups return "" → coerced to null, so when the user clicks "Log to MLflow" from the modelling result panel, the experiment name and model name they configured on the Modelling node are silently discarded and the run is logged under a default/unnamed experiment. findings.title: Modal focus effect re-runs on every parent re-render (unstable onClose/extraCloseKeys deps), yanking focus out of the modal and corrupting focus restoration

findings.title: nameSuffix callback invoked twice per row

findings.title: clusterSnap docstring example contradicts the code's even-length median selection
findings.description: clusterSnap snaps each cluster to cluster[Math.floor(cluster.length / 2)], i.e. the UPPER-middle element for even-length clusters. The docstring's own worked example claims the cluster [250,253] snaps to 250, but for a 2-element cluster Math.floor(2/2) = 1, so cluster[1] = 253 is selected — the function snaps to 253, not 250. The odd-length example ([100,103,108]->103) is correct and is pinned by tests, but the even-length behavior is undocumented/misdocumented and untested. The actual code path always picks the larger of the two middle values, which is a deterministic but asymmetric 'representative', not the arithmetic median the comment implies. Functionally the snap is still consistent (all cluster members receive the same value, so visual alignment holds), so this is a comment-correctness/spec defect rather than a runtime mis-render, but a maintainer relying on the documented example would compute the wrong expected output (e.g. when adding a regression test).
findings.evidence: Line 38: `const median = cluster[Math.floor(cluster.length / 2)]`. For cluster = [250,253]: cluster.length = 2 -> Math.floor(1) = 1 -> cluster[1] = 253. Docstring lines 25-26 assert `[250,253]→250`. No test in frontend/src/__tests__/utils/layout.test.ts or frontend/src/utils/__tests__/layout.test.ts exercises an even-length cluster, so the discrepancy is unguarded.

findings.title: LossChart y-range poisoned by NaN/Infinity loss values (no finite-value guard)
findings.description: LossChart gathers y-values into allVals using only a `!= null` filter (lines 30-31), so NaN/Infinity values flow in. yMin/yMax are then computed with Math.min/Math.max (lines 33-34); any NaN poisons both to NaN, making yRange and yScale(v) return NaN for EVERY point. The whole chart breaks (train/eval paths and the best-iteration line render with NaN coordinates -> invalid/empty SVG), not just the single bad point. The backend demonstrably emits NaN/Infinity in loss_history: the sibling LossTab tests feed `eval_rmse: Number.NaN` and `train_rmse: Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` (frontend/src/panels/modelling/__tests__/LossTab.test.tsx:26,44-45). The sibling LossTab.tsx (doc-comment line 4 claims LossChart is 'same logic') guards every value with `isFiniteNumber` (LossTab.tsx:29-30,61-62) and renders an empty-state when no finite points remain (LossTab.tsx:46-49,64-66); LossChart has none of these guards.
findings.evidence: LossChart.tsx:30-31 push when `entry[trainKey] != null` (NaN passes) -> :33-34 `yMin=allVals.reduce(Math.min,Infinity)` becomes NaN -> :35 `yRange = NaN || 1` = NaN -> :38 `yScale(v) = py+chartH-((v-yMin)/yRange)*chartH` = NaN for all v. Contrast LossTab.tsx:61-62 `if (isFiniteNumber(entry[trainKey])) allVals.push(...)`.

findings.title: LossChart.makePath emits 'NaN' path coordinates for non-finite loss points
findings.description: makePath filters points with `e[key] != null` (line 42), so a NaN/Infinity value produces a path segment like `L12.3,NaN`. Even setting aside the y-range poisoning above, an individual non-finite point yields an invalid SVG path `d` string. The sibling LossTab.makePath guards with `isFiniteNumber(e[key])` and skips such points entirely (LossTab.tsx:83), producing a clean broken-line path. LossChart should do the same.
findings.evidence: LossChart.tsx:42 `e[key] != null ? \`L${xScale(i)},${yScale(e[key])}\` : null` with yScale(NaN)=NaN -> 'L..,NaN'. LossTab.tsx:83 `if (!isFiniteNumber(e[key])) return null`.

findings.title: LossChart best-iteration line: no lower clamp and no NaN guard on bestIteration
findings.description: bestX = bestIteration != null ? xScale(Math.min(bestIteration, lossHistory.length - 1)) : null. Two defects vs the hardened sibling: (1) no lower clamp -> a negative bestIteration yields a negative x and the dashed line is drawn off-canvas to the left; (2) `!= null` lets NaN through (NaN is not null) -> Math.min(NaN, n)=NaN -> xScale(NaN)=NaN -> a <line> with x1/x2=NaN is rendered, and the legend gains a spurious 'Best iter' entry. LossTab.tsx:100 uses `isFiniteNumber(bestIteration) ? xScale(Math.min(Math.max(bestIteration, 0), lossHistory.length - 1)) : null`, which clamps to [0, length-1] and rejects NaN. best_iteration is typed `number | null` (useNodeResultsStore.ts:56) and originates from the backend, so a NaN/negative value is a realistic wire input.
findings.evidence: LossChart.tsx:49 lacks Math.max(_,0) and isFiniteNumber present in LossTab.tsx:100. NaN != null === true, so Number.NaN flows into xScale.

findings.title: FeatureImportance maxVal uses items[0].importance, wrong for negative/zero importances
findings.description: maxVal is taken as `items[0]?.importance || 1` on the assumption that the first (descending-sorted) feature is the largest by magnitude. Bar width is then `(Math.abs(fi.importance) / Math.abs(maxVal)) * 100%` (line 60), which uses absolute values. The backend sorts feature_importance / feature_importance_loss by RAW value descending, not by absolute value (src/haute/modelling/_algorithms.py:620-624 and 639-643 `sorted(..., key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)`), and CatBoost LossFunctionChange importances can be negative (no abs/clip applied; _result_types.py:19). Consequences on the 'Loss' tab: (a) a feature with a large NEGATIVE importance sorts LAST, so its |importance| can exceed |items[0].importance|, yielding a bar width > 100% (overflow); (b) if items[0].importance is itself negative, Math.abs(maxVal) is a small positive denominator and ALL bars are massively over-scaled; (c) if items[0].importance === 0, `0 || 1` forces maxVal=1, mis-scaling every bar. The hardened sibling FeaturesTab.tsx computes `maxVal = items.map(i => Math.abs(i.importance)).reduce((a,b)=>Math.max(a,b), -Infinity)` (FeaturesTab.tsx:46) and guards the denominator with `maxVal > 0 ? ... : '0%'` (FeaturesTab.tsx:91). Existing FeatureImportance tests only use positive descending importances, so this is uncovered.
findings.evidence: FeatureImportance.tsx:28 `const maxVal = items[0]?.importance || 1` -> :60 `width: ${(Math.abs(fi.importance)/Math.abs(maxVal))*100}%`. Backend _algorithms.py:620-624 sorts by raw value desc; LossFunctionChange may be negative; _result_types.py:19 stores it unmodified. Correct pattern in FeaturesTab.tsx:46,91.

findings.title: JSON Preview interpolates column names without escaping, producing invalid JSON for names containing quotes/backslashes/newlines
findings.description: The "JSON Preview" block builds a JSON-looking string by raw template-interpolating each selected field name: `fields.map((f) => `  "${f}": ...`).join(",\n")`. Field names are upstream Polars column names, which can legitimately contain double-quotes, backslashes, or newlines (Polars permits arbitrary column-name strings). For such a column the rendered preview is not valid JSON (e.g. a column named `a"b` renders as `  "a"b": ...`), so the panel labelled 'JSON Preview' would misrepresent the actual response shape. The correct idiom is to serialize the key via `JSON.stringify(f)` (which yields a properly-escaped, quoted key) instead of wrapping in literal quotes. Impact is display-only — the string lives inside a `<pre>` and is never parsed or sent over the wire — so there is no runtime/security consequence, only a misleading preview for unusual column names.

findings.title: `abortRef` is write-only — assigned but never read
findings.description: The hook declares `const abortRef = useRef<AbortController | null>(null)` (line 15) and assigns it inside the mount effect (`abortRef.current = controller`, line 39), but the ref is never read anywhere. The effect's cleanup aborts the *local* `controller` variable (`return () => { controller.abort() }`), not `abortRef.current`. The manual `fetchForPath` call path never consults `abortRef` either. The ref therefore serves no purpose and gives the misleading impression that in-flight requests are tracked/cancellable across calls when they are not.
findings.evidence: Line 15 declares ref; line 38 creates `const controller = new AbortController()`; line 39 `abortRef.current = controller`; line 42 calls `fetchForPath(initialPath, controller.signal)`; cleanup (line 44-46) calls `controller.abort()` using the closure variable, not `abortRef.current`. Grep for `abortRef` in the file returns only the declaration (15) and the assignment (39) — zero reads.
findings.est_reduction: 2 lines (the ref declaration + the assignment), plus removes a false signal that request cancellation is centrally tracked.
findings.behavior_preservation: Removing the unused ref does not change any observable behavior: cleanup already aborts via the local `controller`, and no code reads `abortRef.current`.

findings.title: Manual `fetchForPath` call has no abort signal → stale schema can overwrite newer result on rapid file switch
findings.description: `fetchForPath(path, signal?)` only guards its `.then`/`.catch` with `signal?.aborted`. The auto-fetch effect passes a real signal (so it is cancellable), but consumers call it manually WITHOUT a signal: `ApiInputEditor` does `onUpdate('path', path); fetchForPath(path)` on file select. Because `signal` is undefined, that promise's `.then` runs unconditionally and calls `setSchema(data)` whenever it resolves. If the user selects file A (manual fetch A, unabortable) and quickly selects file B, the path-change effect aborts only its own controller for the *previous* path; the manual fetch A is never aborted, so a late-resolving A response can call `setSchema(dataA)` after B's result, leaving the panel showing A's schema while config.path is B. Additionally, on every select the same path is fetched twice (once manually, once by the effect that fires when `initialPath` changes), wasting a network round-trip.
findings.evidence: useSchemaFetch.ts:21 `if (signal?.aborted) return` then `setSchema(data)`; ApiInputEditor.tsx:154 `useSchemaFetch(currentPath)` where `currentPath = config.path`; ApiInputEditor.tsx:374-376 `onUpdate('path', path); fetchForPath(path)` — manual call passes no signal. The effect (useSchemaFetch.ts:35-47) re-runs when `initialPath` changes (config.path just changed), starting a second fetch for the same path. The manual fetch is not stored/abortable (abortRef is unused), so it cannot be cancelled when the path changes again.
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a

findings.title: sanitizeName omits the keyword-prefix step, diverging from backend _sanitize_func_name for Python-keyword labels (e.g. "class" -> frontend "class" vs backend "node_class")
findings.description: The frontend sanitizeName() is explicitly documented to stay in sync with the backend src/haute/_graph_utils.py::_sanitize_func_name (see the file's own docstring and the comment block at NodePanel.tsx:699-708). The backend performs FOUR final guards: (1) prefix node_ if the result starts with a digit, (2) prefix node_ if the result is a Python keyword via keyword.iskeyword(name), then (3) fall back to unnamed_node. The frontend implements only guards (1) and (3) and SKIPS the keyword guard entirely. There is no keyword check anywhere in frontend/src (grep for iskeyword/keyword finds only CodeMirror syntax-highlight tokens). Consequently, for any node whose label sanitises to a reserved Python keyword (class, return, import, for, if, def, lambda, while, with, yield, global, None, True, False, and, or, not, in, is, etc.), the two implementations disagree: backend produces e.g. "node_class" but frontend produces "class". sanitizeName feeds load-bearing identifiers in NodePanel.tsx: upstream input varNames for wiring (lines 244, 254, 360, 636), and the api_input cache configPath `config/quote_input/${sanitizeName(label)}.json` (line 708). The backend writes/reads these under the keyword-prefixed name. The mismatch reproduces exactly the class of bug the NodePanel.tsx:699-708 comment says was fixed: the frontend computes a name the backend never wrote, so the api_input cache-status GET resolves to the wrong path -> silent cached=false / unresponsive cache button; and editor-displayed input variable names disagree with the names in generated code. The keyword guard is necessary precisely because str.isidentifier() returns True for keywords (so the identifier-validity invariant alone does not catch them) - the backend's own test_parser_sanitize_contracts.py::test_round_trip_stability_on_ascii deliberately includes "class" in its candidate list.
findings.evidence: Backend _graph_utils.py:121-125: `if name and name[0].isdigit(): name = f"node_{name}"` then `if keyword.iskeyword(name): name = f"node_{name}"` then `return name or "unnamed_node"`. Frontend sanitizeName.ts:36-37: `if (name && /^[0-9]/.test(name)) name = \`node_${name}\`` then `return name || "unnamed_node"` -- the keyword branch is absent. So sanitizeName("class") === "class" while _sanitize_func_name("class") === "node_class". NodePanel.tsx:708 builds `config/quote_input/${sanitizeName(node.data.label)}.json`, and codegen.py:546/_save_pipeline.py:229 build the backend-side names via _sanitize_func_name -> the two paths/idents differ for keyword labels.

findings.title: Unused `_ratio` parameter in isConstraintMet is dead in all production callers
findings.description: isConstraintMet(thresholdType, _ratio, absValue, thresholdVal) never reads `_ratio`; its body only branches on thresholdType and compares absValue against thresholdVal. Both production call sites pass the literal `0` for the ratio argument (SummaryTab.tsx:63 and DetailCard.tsx:143). The parameter exists purely as a placeholder in the signature. Since neither caller derives anything from a ratio, the second positional argument is dead weight that forces callers to thread a meaningless `0` and slightly obscures the constraint-evaluation contract. The underscore prefix indicates the author already recognises it is unused. Removing it (and updating the two callers + the test) would simplify the signature with zero behaviour change.
findings.evidence: optimiserHelpers.ts body: `if (thresholdType === "min") return absValue >= thresholdVal; if (thresholdType === "max") return absValue <= thresholdVal; return false` — `_ratio` is never referenced. Callers: SummaryTab.tsx:63 `isConstraintMet(thresholdType, 0, value, thresholdVal)`; DetailCard.tsx:143 `isConstraintMet(thresholdType, 0, value, thresholdVal)`. No call site passes a non-zero ratio in production (only the unit test passes varying ratios, and those values cannot change the result).
findings.est_reduction: ~1 parameter removed from signature + 2 call-site arg removals + 1 test signature tidy
findings.behavior_preservation: Fully behaviour-preserving: the parameter is never read, so removing it and dropping the `0` arg at both call sites yields identical output for every input.
